Illustrative triage: enquiries fall on a day a core update is announced, but the mobile form also returns an error after a website release. Repair and retest the form immediately. Preserve search observations for the later review. Waiting for the rollout to finish would not make a broken form acceptable, and fixing it would not prove the update had no effect.

## Compare equivalent groups

Compare affected pages and queries across sensible periods, using consistent country, device and search-type filters. Inspect impressions, clicks and position together. Separate brand queries, service pages, articles and product collections where their purposes differ.

Account for reporting delay, low volume and seasonality. A change in average position can reflect a different mix of queries. Review the [Search Console walkthrough](/blog/google-search-console-the-operators-guide/) before treating an aggregate as a page-level explanation.

## Worked example: fewer article clicks, steady inquiries

Imagine informational articles lose clicks while service-page visits and qualified inquiries remain similar. That does not establish that the content is fine or that AI answers caused the decline.

Inspect the affected queries and current results. Check whether demand, the search presentation, competing pages or your own page changed. Review whether the article still provides a useful, accurate answer. Keep the business outcome separate from the visibility diagnosis.

| Observation | Possible explanation | Next evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One template loses indexed pages | Technical release problem | Public HTML and URL Inspection |
| Seasonal queries lose impressions | Demand change | Comparable seasonal periods and query context |
| Clicks fall while appearances hold | Result presentation or competing offers | Actual results and query-level comparison |
| Orders fall across channels | Broader business or measurement issue | Stock, checkout and order records |

These are hypotheses, not automatic conclusions.

## Make a change you can evaluate

If the page has factual errors, missing buying information or broken navigation, repair those defects. Record the reason and deployment date. Avoid changing the title, URL, content, template and internal links all at once merely to demonstrate activity.

Some problems require coordinated changes. In that case, document the bundle and accept that isolating each change's effect will be harder. Preserve useful pages and URLs unless the evidence supports a different treatment.

## Review without promising recovery dates

After a repair, verify the public result first. Then monitor discovery and relevant business outcomes over an appropriate period. Google's guidance does not promise that every change produces recovery at the next update.

[Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) to retain observations, hypotheses and checks. The [2023–2026 update record](/blog/three-years-of-algorithm-updates-what-moved-rankings/) supplies historical context; it does not diagnose your site.

title: Google Search Console: A Practical Review for Business Owners
description: Use Google Search Console to connect queries, landing pages, indexation, and structured data to decisions. Turn search reporting into an actionable routine.
markdown:
Search Console tells you how your website appears in Google Search. It does not tell you whether an inquiry became a good customer.

Use it to find the next useful question, then connect the answer to your website and business records. Opening every chart at once rarely improves the diagnosis.

## Before you start

Confirm access to the correct property and identify its coverage. A Domain property and a URL-prefix property can include different versions of a site. Ask the owner for appropriate access rather than sharing credentials.

Write one question: “Why did visits to our reporting service fall?” is specific enough to investigate. Save the page URL, date range, device, country and search type with the review so the next comparison means the same thing.

Google’s [getting-started guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/monitor-debug/search-console-start) explains the major reports. Use them for different jobs:

| Question | Starting point | What it cannot establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did search appearances change? | Performance | Whether the visitor bought |
| Is this URL indexed? | URL Inspection | Whether it will rank well |
| Are many pages excluded? | Page indexing | Whether every exclusion is a defect |
| Did Google read the sitemap? | Sitemaps | Whether every listed page was indexed |
| Is a manual action recorded? | Manual actions | The cause of every traffic decline |

## Compare the same page over sensible periods

In Performance, select Web search and filter to the page or page group you are investigating. Compare complete periods with similar weekday coverage. Use a year-over-year comparison too when the business is seasonal. Note promotions, site changes and incomplete recent data.

Review clicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position together. Google’s [metric definitions](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7042828) explain that these describe search-result appearances and interactions. They are not unique customer counts. A site-wide average can change because the mix of queries changed.

## Follow one page through the report

Have the exact public URL ready. This walkthrough investigates a single service page; a category-wide analysis needs a different filter.

1. Open the correct property, then **Performance → Search results**. Record the search type shown. Keep that type unchanged throughout the comparison.
2. Open the date selector and choose **Compare**. Set two complete periods with matching lengths. Record their actual start and end dates; do not include an unfinished current day simply to get a round number.
3. Turn on clicks, impressions and average CTR. Open the **Pages** table. Find the exact page and click its row to filter the report to that URL. Check the filter at the top before continuing. Use **+ Add filter → Pages** if the page is difficult to locate; choose the appropriate exact-URL match rather than a substring that includes several pages.
4. Open **Queries**. Compare the clicks for each period and sort the difference column to identify losses. Check impressions alongside them. Click a relevant query row to narrow the report further, then inspect its date pattern.
5. Remove the query filter before switching to **Devices** and **Countries**. Otherwise you are comparing that one query, not the whole page. Keep the page and date filters in place. Note which segment explains the change; a country is not a city-level rank measurement.
6. Export the table you are investigating with the report's export control. Save the property, filters and dates beside the file. After downloading, check that the headers identify both periods and that the chosen dimension is the one you intended.

Google's [report setup instructions](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7576553) and [filtering guide](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/17011165) document these controls. Table rows, chart totals and query-filtered totals can differ because of aggregation and withheld queries. Do not force them to balance by inventing rows.

## Worked example: fewer clicks, more appearances

The following figures are illustrative, not ZINC or client results.

| Period | Impressions | Clicks | Click-through rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Previous complete four weeks | 10,000 | 400 | 4% |
| Latest complete four weeks | 12,000 | 360 | 3% |

Clicks fell 10% while impressions rose 20%. That does not prove the page title failed. Check which queries gained appearances, which lost clicks and whether device or country mix changed. A new set of broad questions can lower overall click-through rate without changing the response to your most valuable service query.

For an illustrative drill-down, suppose one visible service query went from 1,000 impressions and 100 clicks to 1,000 impressions and 70 clicks. That query accounts for 30 fewer clicks. It gives you a specific page/query combination to investigate; it does not explain the remaining ten-click decline or the extra 2,000 impressions. Check the page's query mix and the device breakdown before attributing either change to a redesign or an algorithm update.

| What the drill-down shows | Useful next check | Avoid concluding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One device loses clicks while others hold | Open the page and enquiry form on that device; inspect the query mix | Every decline on mobile proves a mobile bug |
| Impressions fall for the same query and page | Check dates, indexing, demand and result changes | A title rewrite will restore demand |
| New broad queries gain impressions but few clicks | Decide whether the page actually answers those questions | Lower overall CTR proves the page is worse |
| Search clicks hold but valid enquiries fall | Check form delivery and lead records separately | Search Console measures lead quality |

Inspect relevant search results and the page itself. Record alternative explanations before editing anything. Then check actual inquiries: a small traffic decline and a decline in qualified demand are different business problems.

## Investigate indexing separately

Use URL Inspection when the question is whether Google has indexed the intended page. Compare the indexed information with the live test. Inspect the selected canonical and the page’s response, robots instructions, internal links and sitemap entry.

A successful live test is not a promise of indexing or a prediction of Google’s chosen canonical. Use the [canonical debugging guide](/blog/search-console-canonical-indexing-debugging/) when those signals disagree.

Not every excluded URL needs repair. Redirected URLs, intentional duplicates and private utility pages can have legitimate reasons to remain outside the index.

## Respect reporting limits

The [Performance report documentation](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7576553) explains filtering and data limits. Some queries are withheld for privacy, and displayed rows need not reconcile to every total. Do not manufacture the missing queries or call a filtered export the complete market.

Google’s [2026 generative-AI reporting announcement](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports) describes dedicated visibility views alongside overall reporting. Inspect the available report and its metric definitions rather than labelling all organic traffic as AI traffic. An AI impression does not establish a click, inquiry or sale.

## Leave with one documented action

Record the question, filters, comparison dates, observation, evidence, proposed change, owner and review date. For the example above, the next action might be to examine newly appearing broad queries before rewriting the service page.

After a repair, verify the actual page and allow for processing and recrawling before drawing conclusions. Keep an annotation for the change. If several changes happen together, acknowledge that the result cannot isolate the effect of one edit.

Use our [query and page review](/blog/search-console-query-page-review/) for the recurring routine. [Business intelligence](/services/business-intelligence/) connects these search observations with inquiry quality and operational records. The chart starts the investigation; it does not finish it.

## Keep a review record

[Download the fillable search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf). It includes a worked comparison, space for your sources and decisions, and 12 acceptance checks. Keep unresolved questions with an owner and review date.

title: How Long Does SEO Take? Track the Work and the Evidence
description: Understand the dependencies behind SEO timelines, from crawling and indexing to authority and measurement. Set expectations around evidence and the work ahead.
markdown:
There is no reliable date on which SEO turns on. A technical correction, a new service page and a competitive market expansion have different dependencies.

You can still hold the work accountable. Agree on what will be delivered, what evidence should become available and when the next decision will be made. Keep those commitments separate from a promised ranking.

## Separate the stages

| Stage | What you can verify | What it does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Implementation | The agreed change is public and works | Google has processed it |
| Discovery | A crawler can reach the page through links or a sitemap | The page will be indexed |
| Indexing | The page appears in the indexed record | It will rank for the desired query |
| Search visibility | Relevant impressions and clicks appear | Those visitors are qualified customers |
| Business response | Valid inquiries or orders occur | SEO alone caused them |

Google's [guide to how Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) explains crawling, indexing and serving as separate stages. Its [indexing request guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/ask-google-to-recrawl) makes clear that requesting a crawl does not guarantee inclusion.

## Set an initial delivery plan

In the first review period, expect a baseline, named priorities and evidence of completed work. If a service page is blocked or an inquiry form fails, the plan should identify an owner and acceptance test.

A reasonable plan may include business-fact verification, a sample of priority pages, technical corrections and a content brief. The exact sequence depends on the site. Do not replace a delivery plan with a vague instruction to wait six months.

## Worked example: an audit is not a deployment

Imagine an audit identifies incorrect canonical tags in January. The developer receives approval in February and releases the correction in March. The relevant implementation date is March, not the date the audit was emailed.

Record the affected URLs and inspect the public tags after release. Then check Google's indexed evidence as it becomes available. If the declared canonical is corrected but Google selects another URL, investigate equivalence and other signals instead of treating the task as automatically finished.

## Explain what is holding progress back

Useful questions include: Is the change awaiting approval? Is the page discoverable? Does it serve a distinct customer need? Is important evidence missing? Does the business have capacity to respond to inquiries? Are reporting definitions consistent?

A new business entering a competitive market may need substantial work and time to establish relevance and recognition. That is context for planning, not a reason to accept indefinite activity without evidence.

## Use monthly reviews to make decisions

Bring completed changes, validation, relevant search observations, qualified inquiries and unresolved dependencies. Compare suitable periods and label low-volume uncertainty. Preserve original publication dates; changing a date without a substantive update does not create better content.

If a core update overlaps the review, follow Google's [core update guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-updates) and avoid assigning every movement to your latest change.

## Agree on the next checkpoint

The next checkpoint should name the decision and required evidence: confirm indexability, assess a rewritten service page, or reconcile inquiry quality. It should not promise a position by an arbitrary date.

Use the [Search Console guide](/blog/google-search-console-the-operators-guide/) and [fillable review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) to keep observations consistent. Good SEO reporting shows what happened, what remains uncertain and what happens next.

title: SEO in 2026: What Deserves Your Attention
description: Separate practical SEO priorities from hype in 2026. Review AI search, core updates, technical drift, content quality, and measurement before changing course.
markdown:
Search now includes more ways to encounter an answer than a list of website links. That changes what a business should observe. It does not remove the need for useful pages, accurate information and a working customer journey.

Use current platform documentation to distinguish a documented change from a proposed tactic. Keep experiments labelled as experiments.

## AI features use familiar foundations

Google's [AI features guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) says supporting pages must be indexed and eligible for a snippet. It requires no special AI schema or new machine-readable text file.

Check whether important answers are accessible in the page, linked from relevant content and supported by evidence. Give each article a useful purpose. Do not create dozens of slight variations because a prompt tool can generate them quickly.

## Search access and training access are different decisions

OpenAI documents [separate search and training crawlers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots). Do not change a site's training preference merely to make it discoverable in ChatGPT search.

A successful request with a copied bot user-agent does not establish genuine crawler access. Security controls may treat verified bot traffic differently. Use available server evidence or native inspection tools, and label what remains unverified.

For the practical implementation sequence, read the [AI-search visibility guide](/blog/ai-search-results-and-generative-search-optimization/).

## Reporting has changed; definitions still matter

Google's [June 2026 announcement](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports) describes dedicated generative-AI visibility reports alongside overall performance reporting. Check the reports available in the actual property and read their metric definitions.

An impressions figure is not a separate count of AI-generated sales. Keep observed citations, identifiable referrals, valid inquiries and qualified leads distinct. Missing attribution should remain missing rather than being assigned to a fashionable channel.

## Content quality is not a detector score

Google's [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) address scaled content abuse. The useful review is whether the page adds value and makes accurate claims, not whether a detector guesses how a paragraph was drafted.

Read the article against its promise. A how-to should provide enough prerequisites, steps and validation for its audience. An analysis should separate evidence from interpretation. Verify author identity and remove experiences or results the author cannot substantiate.

## Worked priority decision

Imagine a business has an elaborate AI text file but a service page with an outdated phone number, unsupported claims and no clear inquiry route. Correct the business facts and buyer journey first. Then verify crawling and indexing, improve the supporting answers and record search observations.

The text file may remain a useful navigation aid. It is not evidence that any search system has indexed or cited the business.

## What to stop buying on faith

Be cautious with guaranteed AI placement, fabricated authority scores, bulk city pages and date changes presented as content refreshes. Ask what the proposed work changes, what source supports the claim and how its result can be observed.

Use service-aligned blog categories to organize distinct articles. Connect related guidance to relevant services without forcing every paragraph into a sales pitch. The [content hub workbook](/blog/build-a-content-hub-people-can-use/) provides the planning structure.

## Leave the review with an action

Choose one verified defect or useful improvement, name its owner and define completion. [Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) for a record of sources, checks and follow-up. Review search visibility and business response over time; neither is established by publishing the change.

title: Duplicate Content: Choose the Right Canonical or Redirect
description: Choose the right response to duplicate URLs: canonicalize equivalent pages, redirect replacements and preserve distinct products. Includes practical checks.
markdown:
Two URLs showing the same page are not automatically a penalty. They are a reason to check which URL should represent that content.

Google [selects a canonical](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) from pages it considers duplicate or very similar. Your preferred URL is a signal in that process, not a command. The practical question is whether the selected page is the right one for customers and your site.

## Identify the kind of duplication

Start with examples, not a site-wide replacement rule. Gather the affected URL, its preferred counterpart, response status, canonical tag, internal links and sitemap entry. If you have Search Console access, record the Google-selected canonical and the date of the indexed information.

| Situation | Appropriate starting point | What to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tracking parameters show the same product | Canonical to the clean equivalent URL | The same product and content remain available |
| An old article has moved permanently | Redirect to its actual replacement | The destination answers the same need |
| Two distinct products share manufacturer copy | Improve their distinguishing information | Each product can still have its own useful page |
| A filtered collection serves a useful buying need | Evaluate it as a distinct landing page | Product selection, intent and page value differ |
| A utility page should not appear in Search | Consider noindex while allowing crawling | The page is not private; access controls protect private content |

A matching title alone does not prove two pages are duplicates.

![Choose a canonical for equivalent pages, a redirect for a permanent replacement, and preserve distinct useful pages.](/media/blog-review/canonical-decisions.svg)

## Canonicals are for equivalent content

Suppose the same blue backpack appears at a clean product URL and at that URL with a campaign parameter. A canonical pointing to the clean product URL can express your preference while both links continue to work.

A collection of backpacks is different from one backpack’s product page. Do not canonicalize the product to the collection because both mention backpacks. That discards the distinction the buyer needs.

Google’s [canonical guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) explains the available signals. Keep your canonical, internal links and sitemap consistent. Use an absolute canonical URL that resolves successfully and represents the equivalent content.

## Redirect when the old address is no longer needed

If an article has permanently moved, a direct permanent redirect helps visitors and search systems reach the replacement. Check that the destination is relevant and that the redirect does not loop or pass through unnecessary intermediate URLs.

Do not redirect every deleted product or article to the homepage. When no useful replacement exists, an honest not-found response may be the appropriate result. See Google’s [redirect documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects).

## Treat filters and archives deliberately

A sort order may present the same collection differently. A carefully selected product subset can answer a different buying question. Inspect representative URLs before deciding how a filter family should be crawled or indexed.

Do not combine robots blocking, noindex and canonical tags indiscriminately. A crawler generally needs access to read a page’s indexing and canonical instructions. Google’s [faceted navigation guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/crawling-managing-faceted-navigation) discusses crawl management for large parameter spaces; that is a different question from choosing a representative among equivalent pages.

## Syndicated articles need an explicit agreement

When another publisher republishes an article, agree which copy should be eligible for Search before distribution. For syndicated material, Google [does not recommend relying on a canonical annotation](https://support.google.com/news/publisher-center/answer/9606800) to prevent duplication. Ask the partner about appropriate indexing restrictions and clear source attribution.

That is a publishing agreement, not a tag you can add to someone else’s website.

## Check the correction

After changing one representative URL, inspect its response, canonical, links and sitemap. Test the customer journey too. Then inspect the relevant Search Console result after Google has had a chance to recrawl; the live test does not predict Google’s eventual canonical choice.

Keep a simple record: affected URL, intended representative, reason, change, test result and follow-up date. Use the [canonical debugging walkthrough](/blog/search-console-canonical-indexing-debugging/) for a step-by-step investigation.

For repeated problems, fix the template, app or routing rule that creates them rather than editing hundreds of pages individually. [Technical SEO](/services/seo/) should leave a consistent site behind, not a spreadsheet full of exceptions.

## A completed URL comparison

These are illustrative URLs, not results from a customer website.

| Check | Parameter copy | Preferred product page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| URL | https://example.com/products/blue-bag?campaign=email | https://example.com/products/blue-bag |
| Content | The same blue bag | The same blue bag |
| Response before correction | 200 | 200 |
| Declared canonical before correction | Parameter URL itself | Clean product URL |
| Discovery conflict | Category links to the parameter copy | Sitemap lists the clean URL |
| Correction | Declare the clean equivalent as canonical; update category link | Keep the clean page accessible and self-canonical |
| Immediate retest | Both pages load; both canonical declarations identify the clean URL | Category link and sitemap use this URL |
| Google-selected canonical | Inspect after a later crawl; not established by the live retest | Record the actual result and crawl date |

If the clean URL redirects, fails to load or describes a different item, stop: it is not yet a suitable representative. A parameter that selects a materially different variant also needs its own assessment. Do not apply this example to every parameter by pattern alone.

[Download the canonical inspection sheet](/downloads/canonical-inspection.csv). Open the CSV in a spreadsheet, retain the labelled examples for reference and add one row per pair. Keep live checks and later indexed observations in separate columns.
